speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the purpose of this bill is to provide a right of action to any class or group of consumers who may have suffered loss as a result of offences under either federal or provincial consumer protection laws or breaches of contract and where it is impractical for an individual lawsuit to be undertaken because of the nature and size of the loss. speechtext: Mr. Speaker, in my statement yesterday I suggested to the House that the movement of the price of petroleum in the Canadian market, the revenues to be derived from any increase in price, and the burdens that might be incurred as a result of the movement of that price were issues that had to be discussed by the first ministers three weeks from now in Ottawa, and subsequently by the ministers of finance, since the international price structure as it bore upon Canada radically affected the whole fiscal relationship between the federal government and the provinces.

subtopic: LIFTING OF FREEZE AT END OF WINTER-SUGGESTED DEFERMENT OF EXPORT CHARGE LEGISLATION
speechtext: If it is the minister's opinion that the whole question of the price structure is not going to be determined until after the first ministers meeting at the end of this month, would it not be advisable to leave the matter of the legislation dealing with the export charge until after that date and in the meantime deal only with the export tax on which we have some specific information?

subtopic: LIFTING OF FREEZE AT END OF WINTER-SUGGESTED DEFERMENT OF EXPORT CHARGE LEGISLATION

subsubtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF PHASING OUT OF SURTAX ON IMPORTS OF CATTLE AND BEEF
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to announce arrangements for terminating the surtax on beef and cattle by February 10. The tax will be phased out in three equal instalments starting January 14.
The surtax was imposed November 3 under Section 8 of the Customs Tariff because unusually large imports of cattle and beef were threatening the stability of the market and endangering the future production of beef cattle in Canada.
The temporary surtax was three cents per pound on imports of live cattle and six cents per pound on beef. Effective midnight January 13 the surtax on live cattle will be reduced to two cents per pound and the surtax on imports of beef to four cents per pound. A further reduction, to take place at midnight January 27, will reduce the surtax to one cent per pound on live cattle and to two cents per pound on beef. The surtax will no longer apply as of midnight February 10.
In announcing the imposition of the surtax on November 3,1 said the tax was intended to deal with a temporary situation resulting from the marketing of large numbers of American cattle which had been held back from the market during the U.S. price freeze that ended early in September. The government at that time undertook to review the need for the surtax within 30 days. On November 30 the government said it had been decided to continue the surtax, subject to continuing review.

subsubtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF PHASING OUT OF SURTAX ON IMPORTS OF CATTLE AND BEEF
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should first like to thank the minister for his usual courtesy in furnishing the opposition with a copy of his statement before the House met. I should also like to commend the minister on behalf of the opposition for the imposition of the surcharge at the request of the beef industry. We were worried about the fact that there appeared to be some

delay, but we do appreciate the magnitude of the problems involved in the imposition of the tax.
In dealing with the minister's announcement this morning I can only reflect the concern of the beef industry of Canada over the actions of the government. It will be recalled that within a period of just seven months the government completely removed the tax on live and dressed beef coming into this country, restored the tax, by the surcharge doubled the tax and now, Mr. Speaker, by this action it is phasing out the surtax and restoring the position that prevailed before this action began in the first place. I think you can appreciate the concern and the chaos this has caused the beef industry in Canada.
We appreciate very much that the minister did accept the advice of the cattle industry and, knowing full well that this surtax could only be on a temporary basis, we appreciate the fact that the government has decided to eliminate it by phases rather than by abrupt termination.
There are two concerns of the cattle industry I should like to bring to the attention of the government. The first relates to the fact that the minister has in effect telegraphed when the reductions will take place. What this proposal does in effect is, to allow the purchasers of the beef products in Canada to hold off their buying until the elapsing of these various dates, thus enabling them to make an additional profit of up to $1 per hundred on domestic beef products and $2 a hundred on imports.
The other concern of the cattlemen, which is of a most serious nature, involves their hope the government is not completely committed to the reductions on January 27 and February 10, because although the cattle market appears to be in a stable condition now that stability is precarious and could be upset very easily. It is hoped that the government will keep the matter under very serious review, so that if stability does not continue the actions planned for January 27 and February 10 could be rescinded or altered until another look is taken at the situation.
We hope this proposal will create stability in the beef market because it is of the utmost importance to the consumers of this country. There must be a continuity in respect of high quality beef at a reasonable price. The fact still remains that, under present conditions of high input costs, in many instances the profit margin is minimal or non-existent. For that reason we must make sure that this industry remains on a stable footing in order that in the months ahead Canadians can have an ample supply of this very important food.

subsubtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF PHASING OUT OF SURTAX ON IMPORTS OF CATTLE AND BEEF
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in general I welcome the fact that the government will again be attempting to follow the policy we have followed for a number of years in relation to the United States and Canadian markets in order to attain a balanced market for beef and other meat products. In this way the consumer will get the benefit of the large production which is possible on this continent. I would hope this practice would be encouraged. I think the brinkmanship policy practised in the past few months by the implementation of embargoes and the changing of tariffs, to which the previous speaker referred, was a bad policy. To shift back
January 4, 1974

to the practical working policy we had before is a good move. We do not know what the effect will be of phasing out the surtax over this length of time in terms of prices and advantages to packers or producers. Certainly, it does give some advantage to some of the processors.
I point out to the government that it has made no move yet toward a real support policy for hogs and beef. This is essential and would be more effective than trying to manipulate the tariff. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) in a speech in Ontario recently, announced there would be a stabilization policy. I thought for a while he had put on the hat of the Minister of Agriculture because he said we should have support prices for hogs, cattle and so on, but he does not mention that in this statement. If we are to have adequate supplies of beef and increasing production, which should be our objective as a nation, then some moves will have to be made in that direction. Until now it has been left to provinces such as Saskatchewan to guarantee a floor price for hogs, for example, and this may be an area which is being overlooked.
The other point I should like to make concerns the relationship of feed supply to beef and hog production. During the question period today, the hon. member for Bellechasse (Mr. Lambert), for instance, pointed out the lack of feed supplies in Eastern Canada and the instability of the market. This is one area in which the government is falling down badly. The lack of policies on the pricing and transportation of feed grains is a serious matter. The interests of neither the seller nor the buyer are being served. The facts can be documented to prove what I say. I trust the government will take note of these important areas as well as juggling tariffs.

The House resumed, from Thursday, January 3, consideration of the motion of Mr. Turner (Ottawa-Carleton) that Bill C-245, to impose a charge on the export of crude oil from Canada, to impose an oil export tax under the Excise Tax Act and to allocate certain of the revenues derived from the oil export tax, be read a second time and referred to the Committee of the Whole.

Mr. Speaker, it is just a year ago today that this session began. It is just a year ago today that a great many members of this House had the privilege of assuming a seat in Canada's House of Commons for the first time. It is a privilege for which I am sure each member is grateful to his constituency. It is to be hoped that each has served his constituency well. It is regrettable, however, that during that year we have had the misfortune to observe a government in operation which has exploited its opportunities for evasion.
Oil Export Tax
The government has exploited the rules of the House and has used this method to continue the secrecy surrounding of its behaviour. It has continued to keep the people of Canada in ignorance wherever possible. It has used the committee system of this House as a means for introducing ministerial statements, statements of policy and long drawn out statements by representatives of the departments. I think this has been done intentionally in order to make it utterly impossible for a committee of this House to function effectively and obtain the information necessary for an intelligent decision to be made in respect of the committee's report. There has been a deplorable neglect by the government of recognition of the democratic privileges on which the work of this House has so long been based. I am deeply disappointed when I hear such answers as we received this morning from the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) when he said he would refer the matter to the minister concerned and gave no assurance that an answer would be forthcoming.
I was again deeply concerned to hear the typical reply of the Minister of Transport (Mr. Marchand) this morning when he suggested to this House that a matter was not anybody's business except his own, that he would let us know what he wanted us to know and no more, and that he would conduct himself in the way he felt was best for Canada, regardless of what anyone else thought. There has been a direct challenge to the democratic system. This has been a shortsighted systematic operation. There has not been any long-range policy. The government has operated on a short-term basis in respect of a problem which is publicly known because it has been written up in the newspapers. It has not been guided by a policy involving long-range foresight and long-range planning. The government has not taken the action necessary to ensure that the nation will have the social and economic policy which Canada deserves. This is a tired, drained out, incompetent cabinet which has led this country nowhere.
I submit to you, Sir, that this government does not have the respect the government should have and does not have the support of the voters of Canada. It has been demonstrated beyond any doubt that Canada needs a fresh and creative group, with imagination and capability for planning, which is not present in the structure of the government today. It is time that we had forthright, courageous leadership which will not be influenced by a Prime Minister who accepts only the advice of those on his political left who espouse ideas which seem to please him much more than the realities of Canada's economy. The indications are that there is a tryst or perhaps even a conspiracy between the Prime Minister and those who are practising socialists in the House, to take Canada along a collision course with the economic reality at a time when others who have learned lessons about the necessity for the exploitation of the best brains in their country have been going in the opposite direction.
At a time when the economic climate for the development of the resources has improved in other nations, we have been discussing in the House the fearsome subject of profits as if that were a dirty word. We have been discussing it in a way which has accused the industry and the private citizen who was seeking to make a living of being

January 4, 1974
Oil Export Tax
capitalist oriented and not interested in the development of their own country. This is a charge without foundation in fact. It is indeed detrimental to the best interests of our country at a very serious time.
The legislation which has been introduced in respect of the energy requirements of Canada is typical. We have brought in a patchwork regulatory type of legislation which has provided no incentive for anyone to go out to work. It has provided no means whereby the resources of knowledge, technical skill and private and public capability could be encouraged to go forward and seek the solution which must be found if Canada is to remain economically viable.
The only suggestions that have been made by this government in the last year in respect of the economic ills which we have suffered is that the taxpayer will have to help bear the burden, and the government will be given a further opportunity to interfere with the rights and privileges of citizens and other governments in such a fashion that their authority and privileges are restricted. They have exhibited no understanding of the value of national or international goodwill, but rather have been obsessed with the idea of the divine right to rule which is so typical of the present Prime Minister and the cabinet which has continued to advise and support him on this course. There has been a continuing concentration of power in the hands of the central government to the detriment of the provinces, and I abhor this. There has been a total lack of understanding of Canada as it should be.
This is reason enough in itself for the public to reject this government. This government has assumed the position that it is responsible to nobody, and as it has taken on new authority through its authoritative legislation, it has mocked the people of Canada, the democratic structure, and the members of this House in a merciless fashion.
The provinces have little left to deal with when they meet the federal government at the first ministers conference. Yet, the government of Canada has in its hands all the strength it needs to say to the provinces: If you do not like this, this is what we will do anyway. It is not an opportunity for real and proper negotiations. The government of Canada thinks it is now able to confront the provinces and it does not have to have, in the words of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner), real and proper negotiations any longer.
I think that one of the typical examples of the unpardonable, incredible and long-term bungling that this government has practised in its last year is the haggling over the method of the development of the tar sands. If Canada were ever in a position where initiative and action were required, it is certainly in the development of the tar sands for the provision of additional fuel for this country. If by any chance all the accusations which the government has made in respect of profits were true, I submit to you, Mr. Speaker, and to this nation, that the government has the instrument in its own hands whereby it can correct any improper profit, and that instrument is taxation.
It is high time that the government took a look at the capabilities of this country in all respects. It should not get itself and the citizens of this country into an improper, uncomfortable and unnecessary position by bringing in

short-term, prejudicial legislation based upon the absolute need of power and the support of the socialists in this House. The governing party today is not interested in Canada. Rather, it is interested in power alone and it has demonstrated this to the public on innumerable occasions, thus creating the basis for its own defeat.

speechtext:
I want to say this, Mr. Speaker. If at any time Quebec had ever behaved in the way that some of our western provinces are behaving, there would have been such an uproar in this House and across the nation as would have been difficult to put down. In the worst of times, Quebec has always been the bad boy in confederation, and it has been at Quebec that the finger has always been pointed. But in my recollection, Quebec has never taken the kind of adamant position against the federal government that is now being taken by the western provinces. Their claims for special recognition and certain rights have always been tempered to some extend, and I must say they have always been far more tempered than the voices of the western provinces. For years it has been the west that has had grievances against Quebec. What does Quebec want? Why is Quebec always making difficulties? Now, we have to ask members from the west the same kind of question.
It may be that some of my friends and colleagues in the House will say that I am not really advocating a federalist position, that after all I am from Ontario and that the remarks I have made about those from Alberta and Saskatchewan probably apply equally well to myself or that I am setting out what might be an Ontario position. It may
January 4, 1974

be so. None of us know for certain to what extent we represent the mood of our province and that of the nation. But I do honestly feel that I am trying to put forward what I think is a federalist position. The west has had its grievances against Ontario. On many occasions when I have spoken in this House I have enumerated them. I think those grievances should be recognized, and some sort of political settlement reached on them. But I also want to say that those grievances have been exaggerated beyond proportion. Too often overlooked is the fact that Ontario has accommodated itself to the needs of confederation, to the need to share the wealth of our society as much as it can.
For a long time when wheat was a glut on the international market Ontario was prepared to buy wheat under a two-price system, under that strange situation in which one of the greatest wheat producing nations of the world was paying more for its own wheat than foreign countries to which it was selling wheat. I know that people in the west have remarkable abilities, but one of their faculties which seems to be under developed is that of memory. We did, in fact, have a two-price system, and we were prepared to pay more for wheat in Canada than we received for it on foreign markets.
Now, when we hear talk about transportation it is as though we never had an accommodation on freight rates, as if there were no subsidization of freight rates, even though there has been massive and intensive subsidization of transportation both in eastern and western Canada. Indeed, the thing has become so mixed up now that no one really knows what true transportation rates are, because one kind of subsidization or correction has been put on top of another, obscuring the real rates.
For a long time now we have had a system of equalization grants by which we try to match the increases and benefits received by one province through federal grants to the poorer provinces. In fact, there has been a very substantial matching of grants, and I will return to this a little further on in my speech. In some cases it has amounted to about one-third of the increase in revenues to a province, which means that as the incomes of the "have" provinces rose this put a burden on the federal government which had to make an equalization payment amounting to one-third of the increases gained by the "have" provinces.
We in Ontario have also played our role in oil, which is the principal subject under discussion today. Again there is a very convenient lapse of memory with respect to the fact that the country west of the Ottawa valley line, the Borden line, for years has been paying substantially higher prices for oil than it might have paid had it got its oil on the world market at the lowest possible price. For 11 or 12 years Ontario and the rest of western Canada, including the consumers in Manitoba, Saskatchewan, Alberta and British Columbia, said it was right that they should be prepared to pay higher prices for oil in order to stimulate exploration and development in the west. Even in retrospect, Mr. Speaker, that was a good policy. Not only was it proper for Ontario and the other provinces to do that, but now we are thankful that that kind of subsidization took place because now we have the stimulation of
Oil Export Tax
the gas and oil industry in the west that might not have taken place had there not been a protected market for that oil and gas.
I am not saying this to register a complaint, but merely to put on the record the fact that in many instances a group of provinces, or in some cases one province, has been willing to pay higher prices in order to help out other provinces. This whole confederation of ours is based on trying to diminish to some extent human selfishness, whether it occurs at the personal level, at the provincial level, or at the national level. Here I am talking in a way that goes beyond my responsibilities as a member of parliament. All my life I have been a Democratic socialist. I am a democratic socialist today. As a socialist, it is my view that there should be sharing, whether that sharing is between individuals, or between provinces, or between countries. That sharing must exist. For me to stand up in a political forum and to argue that any one individual, any one province, or for that matter any one country in the world has an absolute right to do with his or its resources and wealth as he or it pleases, to the detriment of everyone else, would be wrong for me as a democratic socialist, just as it would be wrong for me in the Canadian context to argue this as a member of this House.
It does not make much difference, I presume, to the people who are suffering, to the people who have to pay higher prices, to the people who have to adapt themselves to differences and changes, if the people who are extracting those higher prices are the ordinary citizens of a province or, let us say, the ordinary citizens of Saudi Arabia. Perhaps it makes a difference in that the higher price goes to the people of a country rather than to a multinational corporation, but in the final analysis it does not make all that much difference, because the higher price is being extracted from the consumer. As I say, people in Canada who have to pay higher prices to heat their homes, and who have to reduce their standards of living in order to heat their homes, are not going to worry whether the higher prices go to multinational corporations or to the provincial treasuries of Saskatchewan and Alberta. In either case the higher prices will hurt, although maybe not as much in the latter case. This is really the point at issue here. After so many years of being milked by foreign-owned multinational corporations, and having finally decided to take a stand against them and not let all the windfall profits got to those corporations, are we in this parliament now going to say that it is all right for somebody else to come along and become the exploiter of all the rest of us?
That is certainly not the kind of position I am prepared to take. In a federal system, and speaking as a democratic socialist, I say that the struggle must be one to diminish human selfishness, and to increase co-operation through increased sharing and increased equality of position. In order to do that it is necessary to make sure that those who possess power in some way restrain that power, and do not extract everything they might wish to extract from an opportunist situation. That is the position I must take, and I hope it is the position taken by my party.
Up until this point, I have tended to agree very much with the position outlined by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) when he spoke in the House yesterday. I am sorry

January 4, 1974
Oil Export Tax
that he has had to leave the House for a moment because now I have something critical to say of the minister and of his government. We could have saved ourselves a great deal of our present trouble had the government taken the advice of the NDP a number of years ago. And it was not the advice only of the NDP. I am sure it was also the advice of the hon. member for Don Valley (Mr. Gilles), who at that time was a very distinguished and renowned Canadian academic.
The advice given was that we accept some of the arguments on resource development put forward by the Carter Royal Commission on Taxation. But instead the federal government rejected that advice. I must admit that most of the pressure for rejection came from the multinational corporations, aided and abetted by the province of Alberta, when they insisted that higher taxes should not be imposed upon resource industries, and upon the oil industry in particular. I think it would be worthwhile to recall that Carter advocated that the resource industries should be taxed roughly on the same basis as any other industry. There was no reason for them to be let off the hook. In fact, had that been done there would be no need for this export tax because the extra profits that would have accrued to those companies would have been paid, at least 50 per cent, to the federal treasury.
When we talk about profits, the federal share would have been $21 billion because the extra profits are in the area of $5 billion without export tax. We could have saved ourselves this confrontation with the provinces if we had done the decent thing, but instead we let the resource industries off the hook. We distorted and continued that mish-mash of a tax system we had at that point and now we are suffering for it. Instead of being on the way to resolving our problems, we now have the political confrontation between the federal and provincial governments which may have to be resolved on the basis of the Carter suggestions.
I think the argument advanced by Premier Blakeney of Saskatchewan is an excellent one when he says that the federal government, in the legislation under discussion today, is proposing to deal primarily with the oil industry. Now, when you deal with the oil industry primarily, you are affecting two provinces in particular, Saskatchewan and, more heavily, Alberta. If we are to have a resource policy in this country I think, as Premier Blakeney has said, that it is not fair to deal with one resource only. After all, Ontario gets a lot of its resource income-not as much as it should-from nickel, copper and zinc. British Columbia gets a lot of its resource income from wood and the associated lumber industry. It is not just the price of oil that is rising but all other commodities as well. Why single out oil? If we do not single it out and impose this export tax, these phenomenal windfall gains are going to accrue to very particular groups of people. If the policy of the federal government is to make any sense, we should tackle all resources and not say to one province that it is its resources alone that are to be dealt with. In this sense there is a real grievance against the federal government which would not exist had we accepted the proposals of the Carter commission which proposed to deal with all

resource industries. We did not accept them, however, and now we have a problem.
Prices are always a difficult problem. I know that there are people who are looking for simple solutions and there are various directions in which we can move, but I should like to state some of my personal views. Let us look at the question of subsidization. At the moment there is the idea that the domestic price should be frozen and quite frankly, Mr. Speaker, had the government not moved to maintain the freeze I think we would be facing an election today. I think it is important at this stage, when we are groping for an energy policy and groping for a resource policy, that there should be some interim measures. I see the bill before us as an interim measure, not as a permanent measure. We have to some extent protected the domestic price, and I believe there would have been chaos had we not; at the same time, we have assured that the proper rents are being extracted from our exports.
On the question of subsidization, Mr. Speaker, I do not think we can continue our present policy indefinitely, nor do I think we should dismiss the possibility of a two price system for lumber, oil and gas as an alternative. That is one of the choices we can make, although there may be some difficulty about it. We will, of course, have to accept the idea that prices must reach certain competitive levels. There is some argument for maintaining prices through an allocation system, and for seeing that the savings go to the less advantaged people in our society. For example, when we control the price of gasoline, who are the chief beneficiaries? Admittedly some poor people are helped but the chief beneficiary is the man who drives the Cadillac. The savings in food prices should be passed along as well. On the surface it is very appealing to say that we should control the price of milk but we find that it is not so much the poor people who consume milk; indeed, the bulk of it is consumed by people who are not poor. And so it goes down the line, Mr. Speaker.
It seems to me that if windfall gains and special profits accrue to special groups of people, then those profits should be taxed away and the benefits of those price increases should accrue to all the people of Canada. If we were able to do that in the case of oil, we should do it with everything. Let us assume that a 50 per cent tax rate on the $5 million would give us $2i billion; just imagine what the federal government could do with that. It could reduce taxation or if it did not choose to do that, there are lots of social problems that cry out for intervention. It is not the taxes which are our chief problem; there are the poor in our society who need to be assisted. We could calculate what the average increase in the cost of fuel is for the ordinary person and if it is $100, he could be given a $100 tax credit or could be given a tax credit for food. If he was not in a taxable income bracket, he could be given a demigrant. The procedure would be close to the heart of my colleague, the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles).
In a selective way, we could determine the priorities of our society instead of letting the haphazard incidence of prices in the marketplace determine who gets the windfall and who does not. There are many things that we could do, but we need a proper tax system and we do not have it. My colleagues and I have argued for this year after
January 4, 1974

year. Many of the problems we are facing today would not exist if we had moved in the direction of an equitable tax system. We do not have it now and the chances are that we will not get it for a while, so we have emergency measures such as those before us. For this reason I am prepared to support these measures, not because I think this is the proper way to solve problems-and I am sure the minister would agree that it is not-but until we can find the proper way we must have some instrument to deal with a situation which is in danger of getting out of control.
Let us now examine where the benefits will go. In order to talk about that, we have to talk about the system of royalty payments. It seems to me that one of the first things we should do is disallow royalty payments as deductible items for federal tax purposes. At the moment, royalty payments are treated as an expense. The companies are permitted to deduct these royalty payments from income before they pay federal taxation. That means you give the provinces the right to pre-empt all federal taxes if they choose to do so, simply by determining what the profitability of the company would be. On that basis the province could institute what I call a royalty tax, which would be an equivalent amount, and therefore there could be no taxes payable by those companies to the federal government.
Royalty payments, I think, up to a point are legitimate payments and, up to a certain point, it is legitimate to consider them as a deductible expense. After all, a number of considerations are involved. I am suggesting, however, that these considerations have now, to some extent, disappeared because of the astronomical increase in price. In the normal course of pricing, royalty payments could be considered as legitimate. I have been a supporter of royalty payments as deductible items until the present. Now, we face a different situation.
It could be argued, as the province of Manitoba did during the hearings on the white paper on taxation, that if the federal government were to make available depletion allowances, or limit depletion allowances, that those depletion allowances should not be for the benefit of the company. It was argued that the province, not the company, would lose as a result of the depletion of the resource. The future prospects of the province are being reduced and therefore the province, not the company, should be entitled to the depletion allowance. I think that is a sound argument. To the extent that depletion allowances are permitted, the provinces ought to be compensated, not the companies.
Because the federal government could not see this point, the provinces had to use the much more clumsy instrument of royalty payments in order to make sure that the interests of their people were looked after. The provinces can argue that royalties are used to pay social costs. I am speaking of the building of highways, and the establishment of a transport system, for taking care of the needs of resource industries. Unfortunately, resource industries cause serious social dislocations and disruptions. Therefore, royalty payments are part compensation for the people in the province. In that way, the people are reimbursed to some extent for the pieces they must pick
Oil Export Tax
up after the mine closes, or after the operation moves to some more lucrative field if certain taxes are imposed. This is like paying for municipal services. Nobody will argue that the tax a company pays for municipal purposes should be disallowed. Some will argue that some degree of royalty payment is legitimate and that companies are entitled to deduct part of those payments for income tax purposes. But we have gone beyond that point.
Speaking on second reading, the Minister of Finance said that the tax limit must be increased, because no one dreamed six months ago that the price of oil would go as high as it has gone. I submit that, in view of the astronomical increase in price, royalty payments in future should not be permitted to be deductible items, to the extent that these were so considered in the past. The question of royalties must now be dealt with.
The question of royalty payments must be considered along with the question of depletion, payment for services and compensation. Royalty payments are now a means of appropriating all economic rents with regard to resources to the location or province in which these resources are to be found. In other words, the fortuitous circumstance of the phenomenal price rise has meant that this economic rent has been appropriated totally to the area in which the resource is found, and the federal government has been pre-empted from any attempt to tax. This might be a great system, but it is hardly one which I, and, I hope, other hon. members of the federal Parliament, can condone. Someone once said that he had not been elected to preside over the dissolution of a certain political entity. We are not here to preside over the dissolution of the federal tax system merely because prices have been rising around the world. For that reason, I want to examine the export tax.
So long as the export tax was around the $2 level, I fully supported the position that the entire amount generated by the tax should be rebated, in one form or another, to the producing province. That position did not seem to be unfair or harmful to the federal interest. I felt that that kind of money should be repaid to the provinces, particularly as at least 50 per cent of that money was to be reinvested in those provinces. I fully support the position of the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands (Mr. Douglas). It would be better if we could invest directly in those oil resources, instead of trying to determine how much money the companies need as stimulation for activity, how much money they are making, and so on. Instead of speaking of money transfers, I suggest that we should be speaking of public involvement in future development of energy resources in Canada. I think generations following us will be grateful if we take that position, just as people are now grateful for some of the decisions that were made in the past regarding public utilities. However, that is not the issue at the moment.
It looks as if the increase in the tax will be to $6.50. That $6.50 is calculated after allowing for some $4 odd to the oil companies. That $4 figure also includes substantial royalty payments and substantial profits for the corporations. In other words, if neither the provinces nor the oil companies get any more than the $4, they will still be doing rather well, although I think the provinces ought to be

January 4, 1974
Oil Export Tax
doing somewhat better at the $4 level. Certainly, the companies can make fabulous profits at the $4 level. Just imagine how much they would make at the $10.50 level. So, when we are talking about the $6.50 export tax, we are talking of found money, of pure, unadulterated profits, if profit can be unadulterated.
At the 50 per cent tax level, the federal government would get $2.5 billion per year and the provincial governments would get $2.5 billion per year. That is a lot of money. I do not see why the oil companies should get more than they are making at the $4 level. Of course, the question of the tar sands has arisen. We are told that it will cost more to produce oil made from the tar sands. Nobody is sure how much should be charged; some say that the price ought to be about $6 per barrel. If the government adopted the kind of tax system we advocate, it would not have to worry about needing to reduce the export tax or treating the tar sands oil differently from conventional crude oil. The companies would be taxed according to their profits. The price system would make sure that everyone is treated with the same degree of equity. The companies would receive sufficient stimulation, although speaking personally I would stimulate them right out of business because we would do the developing ourselves. As there may be some difficulty implementing that program for a little while, we must take the second best choice, which is the existing taxation system.
Under our system everybody, the federal government, the provinces, and the people of Canada, would have the advantage of an ample tax base. As I said, $2.5 billion would accrue to the provinces. If prices were to rise, additional phenomenal amounts of money would be at the disposal of the provinces. The arrangement would be equitable, and I think the provinces would be satisfied with their position. I realize that provincial premiers want to continue being provincial premiers and, without being cynical about it, that is their responsibility. I do not fault a provincial premier or member for saying "This is our resource. We have had a lot of grievances and now we are in the driver's seat so it is our right to squeeze." Human society being what it is, maybe to expect too much altruism is not a basis for policy.
For example, I would like to see Canada say at this particular point we are not going to charge the United States the same as the Arabs are charging. I may be accused of being too altruistic. I have made some pretty harsh statements about the United States. However, for us to condemn the Arab nations, the OPEC countries, for unconscionable price increases and then say we are going to adopt that price for the United States leaves a lot to be desired. Maybe Canadians will say I am being too noble, too generous, or that we cannot go all the way. I would like to see my country at least make a gesture and say we will charge 10 or 15 per cent below the price charged by the OPEC countries instead of adopting a parallel course.
The Americans are having the hell squeezed out of them. I do not feel right about saying they are our friends and we will give them some oil, but under the same conditions. I would feel more comfortable if we were to say to the Americans we cannot supply them with oil

because we do not have it, but as long as we can supply it we will not take their last drop of blood. I am not particularly proud of that policy being pursued by Canada. I certainly would not argue if the Canadian government would forgo some of those rents in return for a gesture of friendship and an indication that one country does not have the absolute right to squeeze the hell out of another, even though it is in a position to do that.
The other point I want to make before concluding is that if all the revenues go to the provinces, every taxpayer in Canada will not only pay higher prices for fuel but will have to pay higher taxes because the revenues are going to the provinces. In many ways we would be better off to have the money go to the multinational corporations. It would cost less. We could at least tax them and get some of the revenue back. However, if it goes to the provinces, the federal government, under an equalization formula, is committed to paying one third of every dollar to the poorer provinces. For argument's sake, if the revenue of one province increased by $3 billion, and that could easily happen in Alberta, the federal government must then tax the rest of the Canadian people $1 billion in order to make up the equalization payments and abide by its commitment under the equalization formula. They are going to get squeezed in both directions. That would be an intolerable position, a position with which no government would be able to live.
The representatives of the federal government should go to the conference with some understanding of the real grievances of the western provinces. There should be a real desire to find an accommodation for them. They should also ensure that federal prerogatives, rights and the whole purpose of federalism are not bartered away.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this debate on Bill C-245 might well be one of the most important discussions on the development of the Canadian economy to be heard in the House of Commons for many years. I should like to congratulate the hon. member for Waterloo-Cambridge (Mr. Saltsman) on the analysis he gave this morning. While I do not agree with a good deal of what he said, I do agree strongly with the remark he made at the opening of his speech, that he was not speaking as a member from Ontario particularly, but as a
January 4, 1974

member of the federal House of Commons on a matter of great concern to all Canadians. I was a little surprised that, having made such a statement, he should have gone on to make less than complimentary remarks about people from other provinces. Nevertheless, I think it important to remember that we are not here today debating provincial rights or similar issues, but the evolution of a policy which will be fair and appropriate for all Canadians.
It seems to me that in his speech yesterday the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) did succeed in stating the problem. The situation is now clearly defined. The position, as put forward by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield), is that we in this party support the proposition that the export tax should continue through a further two months; we would do everything necessary in the House of Commons to make this possible, so that the government would not be left without the capacity to deal with any situation which might arise in the course of the next quarter of the year.
It is an entirely different proposition, however, to ask parliament to give permanent sanction to a proposal which would change dramatically the whole budgetary procedure upon which this House has operated in the past, especially in the absence of further information as to what is involved. The Minister of Finance has been placing great emphasis lately upon the uncertainty in the economy. I agree with him that there is uncertainty, and it seems to me this is one of the major reasons the government should not be pushing, now, for the permanency of any proposal, but should be supporting flexibility.
My heart was warmed yesterday when the Minister of Finance intimated, during an answer given in the question period, that he would have something to say about the Canadian economy in the course of the debate. Indeed, in the opening part of his address he said he would talk about the Canadian economy. He did remark that we probably are facing the most unique situation we have faced in the recent history of the economic development of Canada, and that the policies we are going to follow now, or that may be followed now, will have deep ramifications for the development of the nation.
I was very disappointed that beyond those opening remarks, and that genuflection toward the economic situation, he did not say much more about it; he did not give us much more of the government's thinking on what is going to happen to the economy as a whole. I agree with him that we are possibly at a watershed in terms of economic development in Canada. What we do here in the next few days may have a great impact on the way this nation develops in the future and I am sorry he didn't say more. About his thinking on the economic issues. There is no question, now that the energy crisis has evolved, that there is a whole new pattern of economic forces operating in the world, forces we have a great responsibility to deal with in an effective and responsible fashion. The minister mentioned only one but I should like to mention four.
The first thing that has happened as a consequence of the oil crisis, as it is now known, has been a major change in the international balance of payments of a great many
Oil Export Tax
countries. I do not need to review or recite again the difficulties which are going to be experienced and are being experienced by the European Common Market countries, by Japan and by the United States. The increase in the price of energy and in the price of petroleum products from OPEC countries is bound to have an enormous impact, either directly or indirectly, on the balance of payments positions of these countries. But the problem for these nations is nothing compared to the difficulties which are coming about for some of the less developed countries. It is hard to keep up to date with the statistics because prices change so rapidly, but some of the prices now being quoted could result in taking the entire surplus balance of trade of some countries, simply to pay for energy imports.
Associated with the balance of payments difficulties is the fact that the OPEC countries are going to have enormous surplus reserves. What are they going to do with them, where are they going to put them and what will happen to them? Those are questions about which every nation is enormously concerned. Moreover, what happens to the exchange rates if in fact the United States buys energy in the future at the high prices now being set in world markets. The net result will be that the value of the United States dollar will decline dramatically in world markets and there will be surpluses of United States dollars floating all over the world.
If that happens the price of U.S. goods sold outside the U.S. will be cheap compared to the prices of goods from other countries. Will countries be willing to have the United States flood the world with low priced goods and services because of the oil problem? Not likely! The possibility of increases in tariffs along with other measures designed to impede world trade will be great and cannot be under-estimated. The other possible impact of such an international monetary situation, could be, if we have that sort of devaluation, enormous inflation. People keep wondering why there is so much inflation in Canada and in the United States; certainly one of the reasons has been the devaluation which has taken place in our currency in foreign markets. This condition could be exacerbated if the international situation with respect to balance of payments deteriorates.
I am slightly distressed at the position Canada is taking in this matter-one of wait and see. During periods of uncertainty, it is important to watch how a situation is developing, how it is going and how it is moving, but Canada has a long, important and significant tradition as being a leader in the development of ideas for dealing with international monetary situations. I am sure the Minister of Finance will recall that when the Breton Woods Agreement was established it was often known as the "ABC" agreement; The American, British and Canadian agreement. Canada, for a long time, certainly after World War II, was a leader in developing ideas as to how to deal with international problems.
One of the reasons we in this party were very disappointed that before the Canadian delegation went to Nairobi last spring we were unable to get a statement in the House of Commons as to Canada's position, was that we were therefore unable to debate international monetary matters in the House. We felt it was important for

January 4, 1974
Oil Export Tax
Canada to take some relatively positive position at those meetings, and that a debate would clarify Canada's official view. One of the ideas evolving in our party, as the members of the economic caucus of the Conservative party will confirm, was that perhaps Canada could put forward at Nairobi some ideas about an international bank for energy, and this of course was long before the crisis arose. I am not suggesting we had the foresight to see the difficulty, but indeed it would have been raised in this House at that time.
I would hope that we will, before any positive positions are taken by the Canadian government with respect to monetary reform, have the opportunity for some serious debate and discussion in the House about the Canadian position. I would hope that Canada can again emerge as a leader, not a follower, in devising policies for dealing with the international monetary situation which has developed because of the energy situation. It is not satisfactory to always take the position that we have to stand and wait. We should be providing leadership in this important field.
In addition to the problems in the international monetary field resulting from changes in balance of payments positions the energy change has enormous implications for the Canadian economy because of our trading pattern. The three areas of the world which are most affected by the energy crisis are the United States, Japan and the European Common Market countries, and they are the three areas with which Canada does most of its trading. We hear over and over again that 25 per cent of our gross national product is generated by international trade. It is inconceivable to me how anybody could believe, given the changes which appear to be taking place in the world, that changes in our trading partners economies will not have some impact on the Canadian economy. What the precise dimensions of the change will be, is hard to calculate. On the other hand, I am impressed by the fact that the responsible ministers of practically every country in the world involved in industrial activity of any dimension, the United States, Japan and the United Kingdom for example are able to make some forecasts as to what they think the impact of the crisis will be on their economies.
There is little doubt that in Canada at the present time the degree of uncertainty in the business community is probably as high as it has ever been. I would submit to you that the reason it is so is not only a result of the changing positions that have been taken by the government in respect of energy policy, but perhaps equally so because the government has not put forth in any detailed fashion what it thinks is going to happen to the Canadian economy.
With great respect, I suggest that when the Minister of Finance talks about psyching our way into a recession we cannot take him very seriously. How can anyone believe we are going to psyche our way into a recession when in fact there is an energy crisis all over the world? How can anyone talk about psyching our way into difficulties when Britain is now operating on a two-day week? Those are facts, and what Canadians want to know is what do these facts imply for the Canadian economy in the future? Surely, with the body of experts we have in the Bank of Canada, the Department of Industry, Trade and Com-

merce and the Department of Finance the Canadian public has a right to know precisely how the government assesses the economic outlook.
There seems to be a view, held by this government that it is wrong, unfortunate, dangerous, or something of the sort, to tell the Canadian people precisely what the government thinks is happening. On the contrary it would be very sanguine and helpful to the Canadian people to know what is happening. It is unfair to believe that informed Canadians are not concerned about the effect of the energy crisis on Canada. It is important for the government to make clear what it thinks this impact will be. It is bound to be important.
The third effect, so far as economic conditions are concerned, of the change in the energy situation is the adjustment in the competitive advantages among trading nations around the world. There is no question that the change in energy supplies and energy prices could have influence in the long run as considerable as the invention of the steam engine had in Great Britain at the start of the 19th century.
The question is what position will Canada play in the changing world. Do we believe that we should use this new condition as a foundation upon which to build an industrial strategy in Canada? Does it provide an opportunity for new types of economic policy? Are we in Canada, in the broadest sense of the word, to use the energy advantage we have to develop an industrial strategy to take advantage of the energy resources we have by pricing them so that there will be a comparative advantage for us in industrial production? I was somewhat concerned with the remark of the Minister of Finance that when Canada goes to GATT again we must go with the hope of greater co-operation with other countries and for an extension of multilateral agreements.
No one is opposed to the expansion of world trade. The greater amount we can have the better. But, surely it is time to examine what we are looking for. Trade for trade's sake indeed may not be the position we should be taking in the Canadian economy at the present time. Consider the realities of the present situation. It is quite clear that not only in respect of oil but in respect of sugar, coffee and other products international commodity agreements are breaking down. Is it time for the Canadian government to look at the question of whether or not it should be striving for some type of different approach to trade, some sort of bilateral approach to trade. For example, should we be making arrangements with Brazil to make sure that we can trade our products for an assured and significant supply of coffee? Is the GATT approach, which was started after 1946, now outmoded with the changes that are taking place around the world? With the present world demand for resources is the kind of approach we have taken with considerable success in the last decade still correct? I note that a former Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce said recently that the only processing we do with our raw materials on their way to Japan is kiss them goodbye.
Well, that might be the proper policy, but with the shift in the world that is going on the time has arrived to
January 4, 1974

examine our resources and to evolve a system of trade policies that are appropriate to the times. To go to GATT with the same set of policies as we did in previous years seems to me to be throwing away an opportunity to reassess the direction in which the economy should move.
Finally, the fourth great impact on economic activity because of the energy changes is that we must determine a resource policy for Canada. I am impressed by the arguments made yesterday by the Minister of Finance, in relation to oil, as to what an important commodity it is, how it plays such an enormous role in the economy and that it therefore deserves special attention. But time surely has come to look at all our resources in the broadest sense and to decide what our resource policy in broad terms will be.
I agree with the minister that the energy situation is a unique one. Obviously, the change in the price of energy was brought about by the monopoly position by the OPEC countries. Under the circumstances any responsible government has a duty to protect its citizens and consumers from those particular circumstances, and of course we have supported that position right along. But it is not satisfactory for the government to deal with similar instances which may arise in such an ad hoc way. What we must do is evolve a resource policy that will involve all the resources of Canada.
The point I am making is that we are dealing with an issue which is much more profound than the import tax. The real issue with which the Canadian Parliament and the Canadian government will have to deal in the course of the next year or so is how the Canadian economy is to be modified and how will it be changed as a consequence of the energy crisis that has hit the world. We must deal with the problem and decide what in the long run we can and must do as Canadians to deal with the changing situation before us.
Given that premise and that foundation it is improper for parliament to tie itself to a position before it knows more about the problems which are developing. For example, we know little about the critical question of what price Canadians will have to pay for petroleum products in the period ahead of us. Until the government can give some idea of what the pricing policy will be it is wrong for parliament to lock itself into the situation we are being asked to accept at the present time. What is the price of oil to be for Canadians? The policy of this party is clear. We believe in one price across Canada allowing for deviations because of transportation costs and so on. I assume that position has been accepted now by the government because clearly differentiation in prices between the Atlantic provinces and Quebec and other parts of Canada is something this nation could not stand at present imported oil prices.
We are delighted that the government has accepted our position. But what level will that price be and how will it be set. What could the price be? It could be the international price. When the Minister of Finance says he is tracking international prices I do not know what that means. Presumably he means Canadian prices would follow an international price. Whether or not you agree with that position depends upon the position you take
Oil Export Tax
with respect to pricing resources as a foundation for an industrial strategy.
The second possible price would be, say, a price that permits a reasonable rate of return on investment for people who are operating in the oil industry. This might be the policy that the government will follow. Perhaps they could tell us if that is the direction in which they will go? The third possibility which the government might take is to adopt a price system that would be one price for oil and another price for new oil. The fourth possibility is for the government to establish a price that is equivalent to a price for alternative energy sources such as hydroelectricity or nuclear energy. The fact is that we do not know and it is improper to ask parliament to accept the present proposal without knowing what the pricing policy will be.
Certainly, to go into a meeting with the first ministers of the provinces of this country with the current excise tax proposal makes it almost impossible to go into that conference with a fair and open bargaining position. Members of the government and the ministers involved must want-and I am sure they do want-that conference to be an outstanding success because no one benefits in this country from a fragmentation or fractionalization among various areas.
The minister is concerned about the revenues that are being raised, the impact upon federal-provincial fiscal relationships, and properly so. All of us are concerned that it will be worked out properly. I am sure that every member of parliament wants the consultative process to be back in operation in an effective and meaningful sense. In a debate of this magnitude it makes no sense to refer back to the unfortunate circumstances of the past. What we really care about is how the problem will be solved in the future for the wellbeing of all Canadians. So, surely the federal government wants to go into the conference with the provinces believing that both are coming together to try to solve this most difficult problem in an open and effective fashion.
If the conference starts with this bill enacted it may be difficult for the provincial premiers to believe that the federal government is dealing in an open and straightforward fashion. Therefore, I would urge as strongly as I can, given the situation that is developing around the world because of the energy crisis, given the fact that we know the change in the energy situation in the world is creating a whole new foundation for the development of economic policy, given the fact that we do not know what the OPEC countries will do in the next few months, and given the fact that we really have to work this problem out as Canadians together, to find an adequate solution to help all Canadians, that this parliament accept the proposal of the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) that we have an extension of the export tax to the end of March so that the windfall gains will go in the appropriate direction, and that we wait until after the provincial conference before proceeding with the latter part of this bill.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, in rising to take part in this debate on Bill C-245 I should like to point out that we have heard a number of terms used, such as "export tax", "export charge", regarding the exports of a resource industry. The minister has stated in his speech that this bill is of great significance to Canada. We have heard much said about windfall profits, who gets them and where they are going. Yes, the bill is of great significance to all Canadians. It is a tax on a resource. A member of the NDP wondered out loud in his speech as to why there should be a tax on only this resource. Why should there not be one on other resources as well. Is oil the only product of which we are short? We are short of steel, we are short of many things. We are exporting many other commodities as well. Perhaps, we should tax some of these other exports.

subsubtopic: PROVISION OF EXPORT CHARGE, OIL EXPORT TAX UNDER EXCISE ACT AND ALLOCATION OF REVENUES FROM TAX
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: PROVISION OF EXPORT CHARGE, OIL EXPORT TAX UNDER EXCISE ACT AND ALLOCATION OF REVENUES FROM TAX
speechtext:
I hear a member of the NDP
saying "hear, hear" to that idea. I think the government should make its position clear. Is this only the beginning of a new system whereby the federal government will raise money for its lavish ideas so as to gather more votes? Is this the beginning of a new turn that the government has taken? Will they be taxing oil as a resource, and what other resource will follow? Will they tax other manufactured goods? After all, steel is made from a raw resource manufactured in Canada. Perhaps we should tax steel as well as oil. Perhaps we should tax lumber of which we are exporting much. The exports of B.C. lumber went up 24 per cent this year, and the prices of building goods have gone up in Canada. Perhaps the government has that at the back of its mind as it spends money lavishly to gather votes.
These are the questions that the government should attempt to answer. They should pledge, before this bill is passed, that this is the one and only tax and that it will only be applied for a time. The bill does not specify that. It provides that the tax will end at the end of January and then- it will be called an export charge. As one of the newsmen interviewing the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) said the other day, it is all salami anyway, and the Prime Minister agreed. It is a tax, a charge, call it what you like; it is an export levy. The bill suggests that it will commence on the first of February, but no one knows when it will end. These things should be ironed out. Is this the only tax, and will it be applied temporarily?
With regard to the matter of where the windfall gains should go, and whether Canada has adopted the best policy, let me quote from an editorial in yesterday's Toronto Star which outlined some of these problems:
Energy Minister Donald Macdonald says the price of Canadian oil will have at least to double when the freeze comes off next spring, and may have to become only marginally less than the world price, now about $10.50 a barrel.
Are we to believe that the tax is coming off on January 1, and the charge will come off in the spring, as the Prime Minister said in his speech to the House last month? On the strength of this editorial, one might believe that the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Macdonald) believes that the tax will come off completely in the spring. The minister has not said that in his speech. I hope 
he makes his position abundantly clear because we have heard so many conflicting statements on the subject. The Prime Minister says one thing, the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources says another, and now the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) is in the game. He, too, has his own ideas about these windfall profits about which everyone is talking and about what would be the best oil policy for Canada. Certainly, we need further explanations. This editorial continues:
Second, the oil producing provinces are entitled to some increased return from their natural resource.
Even the Toronto Star admits that the oil producing provinces are entitled to some increase. We, from the oil producing provinces, would like a clear definition of the word "some". How big is "some" and how soon is it? The editorial goes on to state the following:
As we have lately discovered, oil and natural gas have been underpriced in past years in terms of their true energy value.
That is a pretty good admission and we believe that the government is now realizing the true value of energy and that "some" is substantial. The editorial goes on to read:
But third, the only long-term justification for price increases beyond covering higher production costs, if any, and giving Alberta and Saskatchewan a fair return, is to provide funds for exploration and development of new energy reserves.
I will deal with that a little later, but first I want to emphasize that even the editorial in the Star admits there is some justification for price increases, and one reason they give is the higher production costs. The Star believes inflation will affect everybody, but not the cost of finding oil. As I say, they disregard the higher production costs, but they do say there is justification to provide funds for exploration and development of new energy reserves. That is a very significant point.
In his speech the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) outlined three points that were similar to the points made by the Toronto Star. He said there were three important points and they were interrelated. According to him half of the total energy produced in Canada comes from oil, and that a sudden jump in price can cause grave disruption to our economy. If we are to believe the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Macdonald) that $10.50 per barrel will be the price in spring, then there will certainly be a sudden jump. Of course, we hope that in spring the heating season will have passed.
The second point made by the Minister of Finance was that the competitive forces of supply and demand have not been responsible for the increase in price. That is a debatable point, and I will deal with it later. Then, he went on to say that 2 million barrels per day are produced in Alberta, and that if we increased the price of that oil by $6 or $7 a barrel this would involve a great deal of money. That is certainly an understatement for the Minister of Finance to make, because it does involve a great deal of money.
When talking about oil we should remember that about 80 per cent of the world's reserves are in the Middle East and north African area. Of the Arab petroleum exporting countries, Saudi Arabia, Kuwait and Libya produce about 30 per cent of total world production, and hold
January 4, 1974

about 50 per cent of the free world's reserves. Recently Venezuela increased the price of its oil to $13.80 per barrel, and the Persian Gulf states increased their oil to $11.65 per barrel.
We must develop alternate sources of energy. What is the United States doing? First of all, it has a two-price system. Even before this crisis came along the United States allowed a 23 per cent increase in the price of oil now in reserve, with no limitation on the price of any new oil that is found. In other words, it is giving quite an incentive to oil companies to find new sources of oil. In essence, the United States is allowing the companies to charge the world price for the new oil that they find. Naturally, in consequence the international oil companies will have a tendency to explore for new oil reserves in the United States. Some 20 per cent to 25 per cent of the oil now used in the United States is new oil, for which the higher world prices are allowed. That is a huge amount of oil, so the incentive must be paying off. When you average the price for new oil and old oil in the United States it comes to about $7.50 per barrel.
What are we doing in Canada? Are we doing anything similar to that? We can say that we have outlined a determined policy to invest $40 million in a national petroleum company. That is a great incentive! That will bring security to the people of Canada, particularly to those who live in the five eastern provinces. Of course, I am speaking facetiously because the people there know that Shell Oil spent $125 million exploring for oil in Quebec and off the Atlantic coast without finding any appreciable amount. There is some talk that this $40 million will be spent on research. I would point out that Syncrude (Canada), which has not really gone into production yet, has already spent $90 million on research, and purchased a lot of its research for a cash price from Great Canadian Oil Sands. Yet here is this great, bold government trying to win the confidence of the five eastern provinces by saying it will establish a national oil company and spend $40 million on research.
How lucky and how fortunate are we? I notice that a meeting will be held next month between Canada and the United States to discuss this whole energy question. According to another report in yesterday's Toronto Star, our oil policy has tabbed us in the United States as being the Arabs of North America. The report reads:
The Canadian Embassy has published a four-page report outlining Canada's oil export policy in a bid to dispell a tendency here to call Canadians "North American Arabs."
The embassy says many in the United States misunderstand Canada's aims . . .
A Canadian embassy official said yesterday that the proposed export levy "raised a number of questions and some explanation had to be made that Canada was not engaged in flagrant profiteering."
The embassy publication says the purpose of the proposed increase is "to help forestall an increase in prices charged to Canadian consumers . . .
The report went on: "At that same time, we were also anxious to ensure that the return on Canadian oil in your market was not significantly less than that being received for oil imports from other countries . . ."
Even they recognize that there is going to be an increase some time, but they are not sure when. The significant
Oil Export Tax
thing is that the Canadian embassy was instructed to do this.
The Canadian government must also realize that if we impose an export tax on our trading partner, the United States, it can retaliate. Two-thirds of the energy produced in Ontario is produced with American coal. I do not suggest that the United States place an export levy on that coal, but it could if we play around with this concept of profiteering at the expense of our neighbour. I noticed that last month the Prime Minister made the statement that in the long run we must allow the price of domestic crude oil to rise high enough to ensure development of the Alberta oil sands and of other Canadian resources, but not one bit higher than that. That is in line with the statement in the Toronto Star. And he said there would have to be some further exploration.
It is interesting to note that the president of Imperial Oil of Canada appeared before the National Resources and Public Works committee on December 20 last. It is the largest international oil producing company operating in Canada, and he is a man fully knowledgeable of the oil industry. In response to a number of questions asked by committee members he very clearly stated that Imperial brings all its oil up from Venezuela, and he did not expect any cut back in supply. I questioned him, as reported at page 43 of the committee proceedings, about the building of the pipeline to Montreal. Imperial is the owner of a one third share in the Interprovincial pipeline system in Canada. I asked were they going to build a pipeline that could supply the Montreal market, and he replied that in no way could they do that. They would build a pipeline to put only 200,000 barrels a day into Montreal. I asked if they would still leave Montreal open to international prices, and he replied that they had to because they did not have enough oil in Canada.
I want to read what he said about that very point because it emphasizes the need for exploration and development. He said:
I thought I had described the situation, Mr. Horner, that if we tried to supply Quebec and the Maritimes with the pipeline extension that would be required, if you went to that degree, then you would probably be looking at five or six years of supply, availability and proven reserves to date.
We have five or six years' supply of available resources to date if we supply Montreal and the Maritimes from the traditional reserves which are 85 per cent in Alberta! Five or six years' supply, Mr. Speaker; I cannot emphasize that enough. Anybody knows, for example, that the tar sands contain huge reserves, but the technology to extract the oil has yet to be developed. Only one-fifth of the land mass involved has less than 100 feet of coverage. He says that we have only five or six years supply for all of Canada if we do not make further discoveries! He goes on:
We would not have sufficient lead time either to bring in the Arctic discoveries or the Tar Sands. We would not have enough development in the Tar Sands to do no more than-
Then, he continues:
Therefore, you are going to run out of crude. You are going to cut off your traditional suppliers-
