January 4, 1974
Oil Export Tax
We do not have great reserves and whether windfalls go to international oil companies or not, they have to go to somebody to develop those reserves. Syncrude hopes to go on production by 1978, but they will be lucky if they are in production by 1980, and they are only going to produce 125,000 barrels per day. We need ten more Syncrude plants in the tar sands if we are to have enough for all of Canada. At page 45 of the committee report Mr. Armstrong emphasized again that if a pipeline were to be built to supply Montreal, another 200,000 barrels per day would have to be put through. That is the amount that western Canada could supply in view of the known reserves there. If the NDP, which is apparently running the government, believes that a national oil company is the answer-and that is one way in which we can prohibit the windfalls going to what we might call the wrong people-then we have to get into the business and get the national oil company producing oil.
In a recent column in the Toronto Star, Jack McArthur suggests that the government would have to pay about $2.5 billion to buy 51 per cent of the common stock of Imperial Oil at recent market prices. Referring to the government he said:
That would make you the leader in Canada but far from completely dominant.
He is quite correct and this is the choice that the government has to make. If they want to guarantee ample supplies of oil to all Canadians, they will have to get into development and that development will have to be speeded up. We have five or six years' supply for all of Canada.
Now, how do you speed up development? You entice and encourage somebody to do the development. But how do you entice and encourage them if you limit them to a price of $3.83 per barrel? It is commonly called $4 a barrel but $3.83 is what the companies in Alberta are getting today. How do you speed development at that price, particularly when development money will flow in the United States and when new oil is found there, the market price will be charged.
The Minister of Finance stated that the competitive forces of supply and demand are not responsible for the increase. At the time I said that point was debatable because, in a way, supply and demand are responsible for the increase. I have before me a pamphlet produced by the Petroleum Society of CIM dated September 30, 1970, the first page of which reads:
On Wednesday, September 23, 1970, Dr. Wilson Laird, Director of the Office of Oil and Gas, U.S. Department of the Interior, testified before a U.S. Senate Sub-Committee on the "current status of the American oil supply situation". In an abstract he said that the spare productive capacity for oil in the southern 48 states and in Venezuela is now almost fully being utilized.
In 1970 it was recognized that the oil in 48 states and Venezuela was being fully utilized! The paper continued: Texas and Louisiana cannot raise production very much further and in fact, all ". . . the lower 48 states are approximately at their maximum production capacity at this time." He noted also very clearly that Venezuela the biggest overseas supplier of eastern U.S. and eastern Canada is producing almost at its maximum potential.
That was a statement made in 1970 by a man with full knowledge of the oil industry, and who was responsible to the United States government, when he testified before a
(Mr. Horner (Crowfoot).]
U.S. Senate subcommittee. He pointed out that we will have to rely on some other sources if our consumption of oil increases. So supply and demand have played a part, Mr. Speaker. As early as 1969 and 1970 we should have expected that oil prices would increase.
Then what about the Arab situation? In a speech which I made in this House some time ago, I said that an oil expert had told me that in the North American market, oil consumption has increased by about 6 per cent per year for several years; that European and Japanese consumption has increased at a rate of about 12 per cent per year; and that to meet these increases the Arab countries would have to increase their production by at least 30 per cent per year. No matter who owned the oil, anybody increasing the production of a non-renewable resource by 30 per cent per year would start to wonder whether it would not run out some time. They have a legitimate right to increase their price somewhat, not as much as they have but as they have said, there are bigger fish in the water than higher oil prices and they are after the bigger fish. But, Mr. Speaker, they also cut back production by seven million barrels per day. Since they produce about 30 per cent of the oil in the world, this naturally creates a shortage. Therefore there is a tendency to say that supply and demand have had some effect on oil prices because of the Arab cutback. Whether that cutback was necessary is another question.
The question now comes up "What does the west want?". A socialist member from the golden triangle of Ontario said this afternoon that for years he had heard the expression "What does Quebec want?". Now, he is wondering "What does the west want?" That made people ponder. Richard Gwyn, a columnist for the Ottawa Journal interviewed Premier Lougheed of Alberta and Premier Blakeney of Saskatchewan and in an article on December 22, 1973, had this to say:
The affluence of Alberta is almost overpowering. New office blocks and apartment buildings tower upwards in Calgary and Edmonton. There is no sales tax, and home owners get a tax rebate.
The article continues:
"All of this comes from a depleting resource," says Lougheed. "The revenues won't last long. We have to use them to build a post-oil Alberta:	petrochemical industries, steel, forestry
products."
Blakeney says the same thing, only more cautiously.
That is to be expected from a Socialist, I suppose. That is what Alberta and Saskatchewan seek and will get. According to Gwyn's column, that industry must come from somewhere. He goes on to say:
Ontario is going to be the loser. Both premiers believe that in the energy debate, Ontario has been hiding behind Ottawa's skirts.
I am not saying that is not right. Alberta and the west want more industry, more development and more people. We do not want to see only central Canada continuing to grow: I do not think it is wise to expect that. The federation of provinces, working under a federal system of government, want to divide up the spoils. The provinces are asking Alberta to do that. We are supposed to divide up our resources, not to be too greedy and to hand out our oil. Alberta says, "Fine; we will do that." But it says to the
January 4, 1974

rest of the country, "You do the same; you give us some of your industry. Move your industry and your people out here. We do not want to see Canada grow and become industrialized at the expense of our non-renewable resources."
To my mind that is an important point. In some ways underdeveloped nations and countries in the Middle east are saying the same thing. They are saying, "If you want our oil, we will sell it. But your manufactured goods are too expensive; we cannot afford them. We need manufacturing industries and we want more industrialization." That position is understandable.
If this country's industrial policy is to be based on our energy resources, it is clear that there must be development in my part of Canada. It is not good enough for the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Jamieson) to say that we will give money to the unemployed, or that we will spend money creating jobs in areas of unemployment. That is not what Premier Lougheed of Alberta is saying. He wants Canada to be built up where the resources are. Our work force in Canada is mobile. Alberta welcomes people from all over Canada. The province is saying, "Do not expect us to supply you with our nonrenewable resources at a low price which does not encourage the further development of those resources." There has been much talk of windfall profits. I suppose the oil companies are making windfall profits. What are they doing with the money? Last year, 70 per cent of the profit made by the oil companies was plowed back into the development of more oil in Canada, not necessarily in Alberta alone. Shell spent $125 million in exploration off the east coast and did not make a significant find. Huge expenditures are involved in the development of oil and gas resources and in bringing them to market. speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, this bill really establishes two very important departures from established practice and indicates a very drastic and new change in our concept of confederation. I am afraid this will not do anything to decrease the drastic alienation of western Canada. The problem raised is that for the first time, at least to any large extent, non-renewable resources belonging to provinces are to be subject to federal regulation in

order to give what is called by the Minister of Finance a fair oil policy for all of Canada, and at the same time levy an export tax which will not be returned to the provinces in total or will not go through the usual channels of distribution to the companies and eventually to the provinces and to the whole of the country.
Let us consider what is a fair price oil policy. It will consist, so far as the consumers are concerned, of providing the smallest price to be paid by consumers of oil and gas, while still making it economical for oil and gas to flow from the ground. Conversely, the producers will seek the highest price possible. It is fortunate at the moment that this oil and gas is produced in western Canada, because it makes it easier for this administration to continue to discriminate against that part of the country. This direct invasion of provincial rights seems to be unprecedented. This tax bill will do nothing to assuage the feeling that western Canada is cut off from the destiny of the country and that its only value to Canadian confederation is as a resource base.
This past year has seen an increase in the stresses and strains on confederation. These stresses and strains have increased, not diminished. The end of last year saw a call to arms by Alberta and Saskatchewan, with governments of totally different political stripe, to make sure they have control in respect of the price of their own oil. The small possibility which emerged from the Calgary conference that things would be better has obviously become a political mirage. Even at that conference the federal government made little or no promise of substance, even as to regional banking and freight rates. Alberta and Saskatchewan have moved to take new powers unto themselves, and Ottawa is finding this difficult. We may become involved in a constitutional battle. Of course, if the oil and gas were located in central Canada, Ottawa would not have this problem with the legislation which Alberta and Saskatchewan are now enacting.
Perhaps it would be wise to look at the reason the world price of oil has changed and how our Canadian situation fits into the circumstances. There has been a worldwide increase in commodity prices. One cannot really blame the Arabs for increasing the price of their oil. The minister suggested there was a quasi-monopoly situation involved, but in fact they were selling oil for five cents a gallon and finding that it wound up in western Europe selling at $1 a gallon. The price- of their crude oil has increased only 16 per cent in 25 years up until the recent increases. The Shah of Iran, as reported in last week's newspapers, made what I think is a very apt comment when he said the western nations had been buying oil for practically nothing and selling them goods at rates 50 times as high as the increase in the price of oil.
As the minister has said, the price of Arab oil at the end of 1972 was $2.50 a barrel, with much of it ending up in western Europe where consumers were paying over $30 for the resulting gasoline. One cannot really blame the Arabs for asking a higher price for this non-renewable resource. We should perhaps also heed the Shah's statement when he suggested that western civilization should not be burning gas and oil in their cars and homes, but should be conserving it in order that it could be used for
January 4, 1974

the manufacture of those things which are so important to our industries.
In addition to the increase in the price of oil there has been an upward revision of the price of renewable and non-renewable resources. I think that is one reason this fair price for oil will create problems. For instance, the world copper price has increased by 300 per cent over the past three years. The price has almost doubled since last year. The prices of lead and zinc have increased respectively by 200 per cent and 800 per cent since 1968. This is much greater than the increase in the price of oil. The price if iron ore has increased by 50 per cent since 1969. The prices of many other commodities have increased substantially in recent years. Nickel prices have increased 50 per cent, grain prices have increased 300 per cent since January, 1972, and lumber prices have increased substantially. In addition, there have been varying degrees of price increases in respect of chemicals which represent over $530 million in exports, with the major source being Ontario and Quebec and oil and gas being the largest base component in their production.
In addition, Mr. Chairman, we export a tremendous amount of electricity, some of which is produced in Ontario by using Alberta gas. Bearing this in mind, should Alberta gas be priced artificially low while Ontario electricity commands the highest possible price on the United States market? It certainly Can be seen that the increase in the price of world commodities and many of our resources has been even greater than the increase in the price of oil and gas. This certainly poses the question: If we are to have a two-price system for oil and gas over a long period of time, particularly when in fact oil and gas can be replaced by other forms of energy in many instances-and the world will have to use these other forms of energy eventually-will this two-price system in the long run be a good thing for Canada?
The export tax applied across the board will, in effect, increase the cost of exports to foreign buyers or, alternatively, reduce the Canadian dollar income to the Canadian producer. If the Canadian domestic price is kept low, the purchasing power of the Canadian dollar within Canada for these products will be increased. Artificially low resource prices within Canada will automatically lead to uneconomical and wasteful use of the resource, particularly in comparison with the situation which exists in the rest of the free world. It also creates an unbudgeted tax bonanza for the federal government at the expense of the purchaser and/or the provincial governments' royalty income and requires a costly bureaucracy to administer it. It does not increase the purchasing power of the Canadian dollar relative to its products or imports.
The export tax on oil has the effect of negating specified prices. It destroys, to some extent, the sanctity of contracts. It is a neat way to increase Canadian income in a period of rising prices and will be just as effective on some of our larger export items such as metals, wood products and grain contracts. But it can work the other way as well. If world prices collapse, will foreign buyers live up to their purchase contracts, or could this start significant unemployment in our mine and forest operations? In a period of rising prices, will foreign buyers live
Oil Export Tax
up to their longer term contracts to supply bauxite or many other products in which we are not self-sufficient?
If a price freeze and export tax is required on oil, it should be equally justified on all other natural resources. A large range of manufactured and semi-manufactured products use oil and gas as one of their major components. Many of these products are exported. If an export tax and price freeze is applied to oil and gas, then it should be applicable to those products which will be subsidized by cheap Canadian energy and sub-stock. Sudden change in the value of base products clearly has an upsetting effect on the economy. Sudden changes create dislocation and require faster adjustments than is humanly possible. I think, therefore, that in the long term the price of oil and gas must approach world prices unless we wish to accept considerable retaliation by our trading partners and create great problems internally.
The price freeze, with all the uncertainty and the problems between the federal and provincial governments, is certainly creating problems for the future in the matter of supply. It is probably only a natural response that most consumers feel there are unlimited supplies of oil and gas at ever decreasing prices. It is wise to look at what the United States did 19 years ago which brought them into this position. At that time prices were placed on products under the guise of providing assistance to consumers. Now it has become apparent that this was a great disservice to the consumer. The incentive for producers to explore was taken away and additional reserves did not keep pace with demand. Wasteful use of energy through the use of automobiles, and so on, permeated the North American economy.
Contrary to what Canada is doing, the United States is taking off price restraints and allowing the market to set prices on new supplies. Record exploration dollars are flowing back to help find the much needed energy. Here in Canada we are following the example of the American administration of 19 years ago. This would make more sense if we had been steadily increasing our reserves, but the last three years have shown a decrease in conventional oil resources by half a billion barrels a year. There is certain to be, until the provincial problems are settled, a very unsatisfactory situation in the structure of the industry.
Then, again, the Mackenzie Valley pipeline must be in a state of great uncertainty. It is generally considered that this would be beneficial to Canada but requires the joint co-operation of the United States and the Canadian governments. But the unilateral application of government must certainly sour our external relations and make the possibility of coming to an agreement on the pipeline much more difficult. It will obviously encourage the Americans to think that the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) are not very sincere and do not have any great conviction that the Mackenzie Valley pipeline could or should be built. This will perpetuate the view of those on the United States side who believe that oil out of Prudhoe Bay should be moved under the guise of the United States flag. Furthermore, with the possible formation of the national petroleum company, all the large integrated companies such as Imperial, Shell, and so on, are a possible takeover. Until

January 4, 1974
Oil Export Tax
the actual framework is decided, the fear of possible takeover is present.
It is certainly small wonder that investment brokers do not recommend the purchasing of stock of the senior integrated companies because they are prevented from going outside Canada, but recommend those small Canadian companies which have acreages outside Canada and which are not affected by the political quagmire in which Canada finds itself. The North Sea especially is attractive. It seems significant, also, that most of these small companies have more Canadian money in them than the large integrated companies which are precluded from going outside Canada. The small company is able to operate outside Canada and indeed around the world. It seems ironic, at a time when we are complaining about the amount of foreign investment in our resource industry, that it is more practical for a Canadian to invest his money in a Canadian company operating outside this country than it is to invest in a company operating inside the country.
I now turn to the application of this tax and the stated intention of the government to keep the price of oil and gas below the world average in order to prevent hardship throughout Canada. However, there are other sides to the coin. Premier Blakeney showed one of these, as reported in a Globe and Mail article, when he pointed out that Saskatchewan, as opposed to Alberta, on the whole is a have-not province except that it does have some extra oil. He points out that as consumers-and the same could be said for Alberta-the people of the province of Saskatchewan depend on the state of the world market for the availability and pricing of commodities such as farm machinery, automobiles, lumber, fruit, vegetables, and so on, which are required by a province with a severe climate.
But this government in Ottawa is saying that it is not right that the province of Saskatchewan should sell its oil at the world market price, and it should be sold at a price related to cost. If Canada is to have a price for oil which in the long run would be below the world price, then this involves really the setting of a political price for gas and oil. If a government must set the price, it will be set on the political pressure of the day and not on any valid market price. A central, national marketing agency for oil will find itself torn between the consumer, who will want oil at as cheap a price as possible, and the producer who naturally will want as high a price as possible. As well as that, conflicts between the various regions of Canada will continue to arise and will become more serious. If these conflicts are not resolved, confederation will become increasingly an empty drum.
I suggest that in the future we should handle so-called windfall profits through a type of excess profits tax. Such a mechanism would allow for further bona fide exploration funds which we need very badly. The minister has said that he has $76 million to give for exploration. I suggest that the federal government is not involved in the exploration of oil and that $76 million will not get it very far. My proposal would not disturb the royalty system according to which the provinces obtain their income and, above all, it would include all the resource companies and all the gold companies which have seen the price of their

product go up three times. It would include the copper companies which have seen the price of their product go up three times, the zinc companies which have seen the price of their product go up eight times, as well as the manufacturing industries which are also making windfall profits as a result of the situation in the world.
Furthermore, if this suggestion were adopted, the tax would not carry the stigma of the present export tax which seems to be directed at one or two of the prairie provinces and these provinces will not be the only ones to carry the brunt of providing cheap oil and gas for Canadian consumers.

speechtext:

He said: Mr. Speaker, Bill C-46 now before the House is one which I introduced five or six years ago, and the government has taken some action along the lines proposed in it. Actually, I had thought of dropping the bill, giving credit to the government for acting in that way and trying to take a little credit myself for inspiring that action. However, as one active in the parliamentary animal welfare committee I am in contact with the Animal Welfare Federation of Canada and I have found from them, from the SPCA and generally speaking from the humane movement throughout the country that there
Cruelty to Animals
is still need for action in line with what this bill proposes. As a result, I have left the bill on the order paper and I am grateful for having these few minutes to explain why I think that at least the subject matter of the bill should be referred to a standing committee for further consideration.
The explanatory notes to the bill state:
The purpose of this bill is to enable a magistrate who has imposed a sentence upon a person convicted of an offence of cruelty to animals to prohibit also such person from owning, harbouring or otherwise possessing an animal or a bird for a stated period of time as part of the sentence.
At present, magistrates are limited to fining or jailing any person convicted of cruelty to animals. The vast majority of magistrates are most reluctant to ever impose a jail sentence for this type of crime.
I have already given some recognition to the fact that the government has taken steps in line with this private member's bill. Actually, this was done when the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) was minister of justice. It would have done a great deal of good except for the fact that the government qualified what was proposed to the extent that persons found guilty of cruelty to animals suffer no prohibition of ownership of animals or birds until they have been convicted for a second time. The power of prohibiting these people from animal ownership is given to magistrates only on a second offence. According to the SPCA and the humane societies, this makes very little sense and I am told that some of the courts are also unhappy with the present legislation. Magistrates will rarely jail a person for animal cruelty to animals. Fines are a most inequitable manner of handing out punishment. A large corporation such as a multimillion-dollar railway company can be, and in fact has been, involved in some phase of cruelty to animals and fined only $100. A pet shop may be fined $50.
The key to curtailing cruelty to animals in this area is to give power to the magistrates to prohibit ownership of pets. For the law to continue to allow the guilty to own animals or birds, thus letting them be mistreated for a further period, is very wrong. As you know, Mr. Speaker, the courts are clogged with various other types of cases. With their limited resources it is most difficult for the humane societies of the country to bring persons to court; and when a person is brought to court he may be released with a warning not to commit the offence again.
It is true that in British Columbia and Ontario under other legislation there is power to remove a mistreated bird or animal from ownership for a limited period of time. But while this may be some help, it does very little to stop the cruelty that goes on, some of it of a rather gruesome nature. What is wanted by the animal welfare movement is a clear provision in the Criminal Code, effective right across the nation, which will on a first offence prohibit ownership or possession of animals or birds for a period of at least, I would say, two years.
There is every protection now in the law for the convicted party to appeal. His rights are well protected in the ordinary way under the present judicial system. Prohibition of ownership is the one effective and exemplary punishment which will ease the suffering of so many birds and animals that are in captivity.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROHIBIT OWNERSHIP OF PETS BY PERSONS CONVICTED OF CRUELTY TO ANIMALS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it seems rather ironic that I, who introduced an amendment to Bill C-2, wish to take part in the debate on Bill C-46 aimed at preventing cruelty to animals.
I would like at this point to congratulate the hon. member for Surrey-White Rock (Mr. Mather) for introducing Bill C-46. However I think we should undertake the education of society at large which is rather indifferent about charges laid as regards cruelty to animals.
I more particularly refer to clause 1 of the bill. It is quite commendable, as I said, and I quote:
(7) -the Court may, if it thinks fit, prohibit such person from owning, harbouring, or otherwise possessing any animal, bird, domestic or otherwise, for a period not exceeding two months-
This is the case of a person who has been sentenced previously.
In fact, who will ever go to the police to complain that such a person, previously convicted of an offence, has an animal or a bird at home? It takes a dreamer to introduce such a clause, unless the public is really concerned about eliminating cruelty to animals.
I must say again that I am fully in agreement with the purpose of the bill introduced by the hon. member for Surrey-White Rock. I hope this bill will not end up the way of most private bills, but be referred to the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs.
It is interesting to note the way people react the cruelty to animals. We have daily evidence of this. On the highways of the province of Quebec, on the great many occasions when an animal has just been hit, how many people will stop to give assistance to the wounded animal? More often than not, a second vehicle fails to stop, runs over the animal and puts it out of its misery.
I now come back to Bill C-46. It is all very well to pass legislation to prevent cruelty but if nobody bothers to lodge a complaint against those who are cruel to animals what is going to be the use of this legislation?
I remember a few years ago going to the country where I happened to see a horse which was blind in one eye. I asked neighbours how come that poor animal had only one eye. I was simply told his owner got mad one day and struck it in the eye. I noted with great stupefaction that no one among that farmer's neighbours had filed a complaint with the police department to have action taken against that farmer who had been cruel to his horse.

Another time in Quebec City I heard about two children who had been very cruel to a cat. They had poured gasoline over the poor cat, then with a match set him on fire and the poor cat was burnt alive. The parents of those children never stopped to think about the poor animal. So once again this Bill C-46 is very commendable but people would have to be educated, particularly children.
I would not want to spend undue time on this because I would like very much this bill to be referred to the Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs. I now stop at clause 1(8) where one can read:
(8) Everyone who owns, harbours or otherwise possesses any animal or bird, domestic or otherwise, during a period for which he is under prohibition as provided is guilty of an offence punishable on summary conviction-
Once again how is this provision going to be applied? If people do not even care about helping injured animals on roads or in farm yards how are the provisions of such a bill going to be enforced? I leave that matter to the hon. member's consideration, and again I congratulate him for aiming at preventing cruelty to animals, but in my opinion the enforcement of the bill seems a little questionable.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the subject matter of Bill C-46 is one which is dear to the heart, I am sure, of every member of the House. Indeed, it is a subject matter which can be of far more significance than one might ordinarily ascribe to it. I believe a good deal of the essential character of any society can be learned from an examination of that society's laws with respect to the treatment of animals. If a society, through its laws on the subject, demonstrates a deep respect for the well-being of animals, it can be a reliable indicator that that society is well advanced in human values. The degree of sensitivity and humanity of any society can, in significant measure, be judged by its laws on the treatment of animals. We recall the sage test of simpler times: You may know a good deal of a man's character by the way in which he treats his horses.
Fortunately, I believe our present Canadian law on the treatment of animals reflects well upon Canadian society. Our concerns in this respect, as reflected in our laws in this regard, are well advanced. Our criminal law prohibits anyone from causing or permitting unnecessary pain or suffering or injury to animals or birds; it prohibits abandoning animals in distress, or wilfully neglecting to provide suitable accommodation, food, care and shelter; it prohibits gaming with animals, animal fights for gaming purposes, and so on.
Also, I believe it added appreciably to the law when four years ago the Criminal Code was amended by this government to empower a judge to prohibit a person from owning or possessing an animal or a bird if that person had demonstrated vicious or cruel conduct toward animals. The amendments contained in Bill C-46 would not in themselves substantially alter the current state of the law but would bring about some minor changes. I think none of us would want to argue with the general purport of the bill to strengthen the sanction and deterrence against abuse to animals. In so far as these amend-
January 4, 1974

ments would affect that general purport, they would receive my wholehearted support. I believe there is some merit in some aspects of the bill, but unfortunately it seems to me that merit is combined with a principle which is essentially unacceptable.
I can see some merit in permitting a judge to order that a person be prohibited from owning or having in his custody an animal or a bird if that person is convicted of cruelty to the animal or the bird. At present, the law allows the judge to prohibit a person from owning or possessing an animal or a bird only on a second, third, fourth or subsequent conviction for cruelty. There may be some merit in giving a judge the power to prohibit ownership or possession by a person upon his first conviction, but combined with that I see in the bill a principle which always has been fraught with danger and one in respect of which we should always in this House proceed only with the greatest care and caution, and that is the principle of minimum penalties.
Under the present law, if a man is convicted for a second time of cruelty to an animal the judge may prohibit that person from owning or possessing an animal for a period of up to two years. And if the person who is the subject of a prohibition order of that kind breaches that order by taking possession or ownership of an animal while under prohibition, then he is guilty of an additional offence and may be fined up to $500 and imprisoned for a period of up to six months. You will note that the present penalty for disregarding an order of prohibition made by a judge is a fine of up to $500 and/or imprisonment of up to six months. In both cases the penalty is defined in terms of maximum; that is, a maximum fine of $500 and a maximum term of imprisonment of six months.
This is the case with all summary conviction offences. Every summary conviction offence under the Criminal Code, including this summary conviction offence-that is, cruelty to animals-carries with it the penalty of a fine up to a maximum of $500 and/or imprisonment up to a maximum of six months. The bill before the House would alter the penalty on breach of a prohibition order against ownership after conviction. It would impose a minimum fine of $250 and would empower the judge to impose a term of imprisonment for a minimum period of three months. In other words, it would remove the discretion which is currently vested in the judge. If he found the man guilty, he would have to fine him at least $250, and if he imposed a term of imprisonment it would have to be for at least three months. That would be the case, totally irrespective of the circumstances surrounding the commission of the crime.
One can readily see that this amendment removes the flexibility which traditionally is vested in the judge, to fit the sentence to the crime. The seriousness of the crime can range all the way from a rather slight and technical breach of the law to a blatant and horrendous disregard for it. By and large, our law has adopted the principle of permitting the maximum flexibility for judges to impose a sentence which fits the seriousness of the crime. Under the present law we say to the court, in effect, that if a person is convicted of breaching an order of prohibition against owning an animal, it may impose a fine on that
Cruelty to Animals
person of whatever amount it considers to be appropriate, given the seriousness of the offence, and may impose a term of imprisonment from one day, in the case of less serious circumstances, up to as much as six months in the most serious circumstances.
Throughout, it is left to the court to determine what the sentence should be in accordance with the seriousness and the circumstances of the offence. And throughout, of course, the decision by the court is subject to appeal either by the Crown or by the aggrieved person. It is this principle which would be altered if Bill C-46 in its present form were to be approved. It would remove the flexibility in the court to fit the sentence to the seriousness of the crime. It would force the court to impose a minimum sentence of $250 and, in the case of imprisonment, to a minimum term of three months. That sentence may in a particular case be far too severe. In yet another case and in other circumstances it may be far too lenient. By and large and in a general kind of way we have always resisted building into our criminal law precisely defined penalties, as opposed to defining certain parameters within which our courts are left with discretion to be exercised according to the seriousness of the particular offence.
As to the proposed penalty for breach of a prohibition order with respect to this particular crime, I seriously question whether a minimum penalty is really justified. Without in any way condoning cruelty to animals, which is a reprehensible act and ought always to be subject to punishment, I think it is necessary to keep the offence in proper perspective. If a minimum penalty is called for here, then the penalty for many other seriously anti-social acts would have to be reconsidered.
It may display less a faith than is justified in the good sense of the judiciary of our country to prescribe minimum penalties for a situation where there has been flagrant disregard of an order of prohibition made by the court. Indeed, I believe that if we were to accept the principle of minimum penalties with respect to this particular crime, that is, with respect to the crime of cruelty to animals, we would have to reassess the penalties that apply to all summary conviction offences under the Criminal Code. I do not think one could justify the imposition of minimum fines and minimum terms of imprisonment with respect to this particular crime and not have similar minimums in respect of other summary conviction offences which may indeed be more serious than this one. It is for this reason that I say before we accept this principle in the bill we ought to have a full and complete understanding of how it affects other sections of the Criminal Code and other offences.
Let me illustrate my point, Mr. Speaker, with but one example. Under section 245 it is an offence punishable by summary conviction to assault someone else. The penalty for common assault is a fine of up to $500 and a term of imprisonment of up to six months. There is no minimum fine and no minimum period of imprisonment prescribed by the Criminal Code for an assault. I question whether it would be defensible to have a minimum fine and a minimum term of imprisonment for breach of a prohibition order against owning an animal and not have a similar minimum or, indeed, a lesser penalty for assaulting another human being. This is the kind of conflict which I

Cruelty to Animals
see would be introduced into the sentencing provisions of the Criminal Code if Bill C-46 as presently drafted were to pass this House.
That is why I said at the outset, Mr. Speaker, that while I see some merit in the bill and while I laud the intention of the proposed amendment, I find some portions of it, the one providing minimum penalties in particular, to be quite unacceptable. Before accepting the proposition of a minimum penalty in the case of a prohibition, I think all members would want to see how this would affect other summary conviction offences in the Criminal Code.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROHIBIT OWNERSHIP OF PETS BY PERSONS CONVICTED OF CRUELTY TO ANIMALS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I commend the hon. member for Surrey-White Rock (Mr. Mather) for the legislation he has brought forward. We have come to expect from the hon. member legislation and motions to do with the safety of motor vehicles and anti-smoking campaigns. Today the hon. member has brought forward Bill C-46 which seeks to provide an additional penalty to be added under section 402 of the Criminal Code with respect to people who are cruel to animals. Frankly, I am not as hung up on the problem of a minimum penalty as my colleague seems to be. Actually, the individual with whom we are concerned already will have had one chance. He already will have been convicted and fined a certain amount or given a certain sentence in accordance with the facts in the first instance.
I think it is proper to provide for maximum penalties so that judges and magistrates may exercise the greatest discretion in determining the penalty to be imposed for an offence. Once an individual has been found guilty, and disobeys a court order, he may be subject to further penalty. If an individual disobeys an order of a civil court, he may be held in contempt of court. Here we are speaking of an individual who violates a specific court order which requires him not to do something specific. He has already committed a criminal offence. He has already had his first opportunity. He has been given a trial and the discretion of the court has been exercised. In all probability, as the hon. member suggested, the result was a fine. Notwithstanding being given all these opportunities in the first instance, he then violates or in effect contravenes the order or judgment of the court and he is now faced with a minimum fine.
The amendment proposes that the law says, in effect, to the individual, "You have had your first chance. You will have your second chance, but in that situation you know what you will face. You will not face a judge who is lenient, who does not like animals or cannot be bothered with this kind of thing." No judge or magistrate will be able to fine someone $1 or $10 or say, "Don't let it happen again." The individual knows when he contravenes the

order that he will face a particular minimum fine. The judge has no option; he must at least impose that minimum fine.
If this had appeared in section 7 of the amendment I would have agreed, but when it appears in the second section where the individual has already had his opportunity, I think it is appropriate that this particular sentence should apply. I do not know that the analogy is complete, but I know that in the days when I used to practice law and defend people on impaired driving charges, a magistrate had a particular discretion on the first offence: on the second offence it was an automatic jail term. I remember on one occasion hoping that my client would not be convicted of impaired driving because drunk driving was a first offence and he would only go to jail for seven days, whereas on a second conviction for impaired driving he would have gone to jail for 14 days. My point is that on the second offence there is a good case to be made for establishing a minimum penalty.
It bespeaks well of this country that we have in the Criminal Code a section dealing with individuals who commit the offence of cruelty to animals or birds: from the explanatory notes this goes from (a) to (g) and applies to people who do various things wilfully, without reasonable excuse, and so on, and the action they take in one form or another which results in pain or suffering to animals. It bespeaks well that we have in our Criminal Code provisions to protect animals that are unable to protect themselves or are not able to speak on their own behalf. The country is right in having this kind of legislation in the Criminal Code.
I think the amendment proposed by the hon. member is good. For my part, I would like to see more discretion in respect of offences of this nature where an individual who has done something such as abusing an animal would not have the privilege or the opportunity of having an animal in his possession for a certain period of time. Where a person has committed vandalism, that individual should repair the vandalism, be it writing on a school wall, a broken window or vandalism to any public building. The magistrate should have the opportunity to say to the individual that he must Testify the damage he has done. That seems to be the way the law is heading.
I have yet to learn of this type of punishment being criticized by the general public. I know we read more of this in the United States. When a person is convicted of drunk driving, the judge may indicate that he must attent a school of safe driving for the next year or two and lectures on why persons should not mix drinking and driving. That is a much more effective penalty than simply paying a fine. In a positive way judges are reacting to what society is demanding. The individual must not only do these things which are punitive but he must learn something.
I remember reading a placard in front of a Presbyterian church in my area. Different sayings are put up from day to day. On one occasion it read, "If you would learn something, teach it to others." That is the type of punishment the hon. member is suggesting under amendments (7) and (8) to section 402 of the Criminal Code. I feel that when an individual has committed an offence and is guilty of committing a second offence violating a court

order, he should know at the outset he is facing a minimum penalty or a minimum sentence. He knows he starts from there and works down, if you will.
I commend the hon. member. I know there are others who want to speak on this bill. I thought I should make the point that I am happy we have this legislation before us. I am pleased to see this type of amendment. Whether the bill or the subject matter of the bill goes to the committee does not bother me too much. I see some hon. members on the edge of their seats waiting to participate in this very important debate. Bearing this in mind, I will resume my seat.

speakeroldname: Mr. Albert Bechard (Bonaventure-fles de la Madeleine):
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROHIBIT OWNERSHIP OF PETS BY PERSONS CONVICTED OF CRUELTY TO ANIMALS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to congratulate the hon. member for Surrey-White Rock (Mr. Mather) for his fine initiative, which is not the first as regards this issue, and I should also like to make a few comments on Bill C-46 sponsored by the hon. member for Surrey-White Rock during the few minutes allotted to me.
At this stage, Mr. Speaker, it would be appropriate to remind the House of the scope of Criminal Code section 402 to which the bill being examined this afternoon refers. Section 402 of the Criminal Code stipulates that:
(1)	Every one commits an offence who
(a)	wilfully causes or, being the owner, wilfully permits to be caused unnecessary pain, suffering or injury to an animal or bird,
(b)	by wilful neglect causes damage or injury to animals or birds while they are being driven or conveyed,
(c)	being the owner or the person having the custody or control of a domestic animal or bird or an animal or bird wild by nature that is in captivity, abandons it in distress or wilfully neglects or fails to provide suitable and adequate food, water, shelter and care for it,
(d)	in any manner encourages, aids or assists at the fighting or baiting of animals or birds,
(e)	wilfully, without reasonable excuse, administers a poisonous or injurious drug or substance to a domestic animal or bird or an animal or bird wild by nature that is kept in captivity or being the owner of such an animal or bird, wilfully permits a poisonous or injurious drug or substance to be administered to it,
(f)	promotes, arranges, conducts, assists in, receives money for, or takes part in a meeting, competition, exhibition, pastime, practice, display, or event at or in the course of which captive birds are liberated by hand, trap, contrivance or any other means for the purpose of being shot when they are liberated, or
Mr. Speaker, although I may seem to wish to extend the debate on this matter, I believe that it is important and relevant to know what section 402 stipulates since the hon. member for Surrey-White Rock wants us to amend it. I continue the quotation:
(g)	being the owner, occupier, or person in charge of any premises, permits the premises or any part thereof to be used for a purpose mentioned in paragraph (f).
(2)	Every one who commits an offence under subsection (1) is guilty of an offence punishable on summary conviction.
Consequently, Mr. Speaker, anyone found guilty of offences such as those I have just mentioned and as described under Criminal Code section 402 is guilty of a criminal offence and punishable on summary conviction. This means, therefore, that in fact anyone found guilty of one of the acts described under section 402 can be con-
Cruelty to Animals
demned to a fine of up to $500, to six months in jail or both.
In addition, under the law as it presently stands, the judge who hears the case has the power to prohibit a person convicted of an offence for a second or any subsequent time from owning or having custody of a bird or animal. The bill before us would change the present law in two respects. One of these proposed changes is of minor concern but the other, I submit, has broader implications and should be fully understood before receiving the approval of this august House. Before discussing the two proposed changes in detail I wish briefly to comment on the history of the current law.
Hon. members will recall that prior to 1969 a judge, on convicting a person of cruelty to an animal or a bird, had no power to prohibit that person from continuing to own or keep animals or birds. Even though a person might have been convicted three or four times of cruelty to an animal or a bird, even though a person might be notorious for his mistreatment of animals or birds, a judge had no power to stop such a person from owning or keeping an animal. In order to rectify this situation an amendment was made to the Criminal Code in 1969. The then minister of justice, under whom I had the honour to work, stated before the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs on March 18, 1969:
The purpose here is to give us some more effective way of curbing cruelty to animals. Prosecution in itself appears not to have stopped convicted persons pursuing the practice of being cruel to animals. We want the power to prohibit anybody who has been convicted on two or more occasions from owning an animal.
Perhaps it is due to the hard work of the hon. member for Surrey-White Rock (Mr. Mather) that the then minister of justice, now Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner), put forward that amendment to the Criminal Code. Parliament accepted the proposition and amended the Criminal Code accordingly. I understand there is no jurisprudence since the amendment to section 402 which would indicate that the amendment has not been sufficient to achieve its purpose.
As the law now stands, then, anyone convicted of cruelty to an animal or a bird can be fined an amount up to $500. In addition, the judge may order the person convicted to be jailed for up to six months. In the case of a second offence, the judge may again fine the defendant up to $500 and impose a prison term of up to six months. In addition, the judge may prohibit that person from owning or having in his custody an animal or a bird for a period of up to two years.
How would the bill we are discussing affect the present law? In the first place, it would empower a judge to make an order prohibiting a person from owning or having in his custody an animal or a bird for a period not exceeding two months, on a first conviction, not exceeding six months on a second conviction, and not exceeding two years on a third or subsequent conviction. In other words, the first proposed amendment would permit a judge to prohibit on a first conviction rather than on only a second or subsequent conviction. Second, it would precisely

January 4, 1974
Cruelty to Animals
define the period of prohibition, whereas the present law empowers the judge to prohibit for whatever period he considers proper up to two years. In addition, the bill would provide for a fine of not less than $250 or imprisonment for not less than three months, or both, for breach of a prohibition order.
The first of these amendments is, I think, of somewhat small significance. Of far greater significance is the limitation which would be imposed upon a judge in ordering a period of prohibition. Instead of the judge having leeway up to as much as two years, he would by virtue of the passage of this bill be restricted to prohibiting the person from owning an animal or a bird for not more than six months on a second conviction, not more than two years on a third conviction, and not more than two months on a first conviction. The question here is whether it is desirable to impose this kind of limitation on the discretion of the judge.
Let me give an example to show the application of the present law and how it would differ if it were amended by Bill C-46. Supposing a man were convicted today of cruelty to his dog because he kicked it: under the present law the judge would probably fine the man and warn him that if he was convicted again he would be liable to a fine or a term of imprisonment, and in addition could be prohibited from owning an animal or a bird for a period of up to two years. Supposing, then, three months later the same man was again convicted for having similarly beaten the dog to within an inch of its life: under the present law, not amended by Bill C-46, the judge would have the power to fine that man up to $500, place him in prison for a period of up to six months, and in addition he would have the power to prohibit the man from owning a dog for up to two years. That is as the law stands at present.
Under the amendment proposed by the hon. member in Bill C-46, on a second conviction of that man for beating his dog the judge would continue to have the power to fine him $500 and impose a term of imprisonment, but he would be limited to prohibiting the man from owning an animal for a period of six months only. No matter how cruel and vicious the attack on the second occasion, the judge, under this amendment, would be limited to prohibiting that person from owning an animal for six months. Under the present law the judge would have the power to prohibit him from owning an animal for up to two years. In view of what I have just pointed out, I do not know what purpose Bill C-46 would serve. That is why I question whether he would want to, in effect, tie the hands of the judge in this way in respect of a second conviction.
Of far more consequence than either of these results that would flow from the amendment proposed by the hon. member for Surrey-White Rock in Bill C-46 is the proposal to provide for a minimum fine and a minimum term of imprisonment for breach of an order of prohibition. I say this is of far more significance because it introduces into the Criminal Code in respect of this offence a minimum fine and a minimum term of imprisonment. Having done this, you remove any discretion from the judge who has heard the case. I think this is the kind of change which ought to be fully understood and completely considered by the House before the principle is accepted.

Mr. Speaker, during the few seconds left I would like to remind the House that the debate on the bill introduced by the member for Surrey-White Rock reminds me how you can go too far when you sympathize exceedingly with animals' plight. I do not mean to speak against the hon. member's bill or that I am in favour of cruelty to animals. On the contrary, I have at home a few animals which I would not like to be mistreated and which I would never dare to mistreat myself.
However I would remind the House how emotions may be exaggerated when an animal is being mistreated or killed. This reminds me of the foolish propaganda made in connection with the so-called killing and in fact the hunting of seals in the Gulf of St. Lawrence. Totally rigged films were shown as propaganda throughout Europe showing how Canadians could be cruel to animals. And I do say that those films were totally rigged. I am very much involved in this since in my constituency as in several parts of the Maritimes seal hunting is each spring a welcome crop which brings money into the pockets of the poor fishermen who lived through winter thanks to unemployment benefits and social welfare.
You know how harmful this has been to the population of the Maritime provinces and mainly of the Magdalen Islands. This is why I do not want to go overboard about hunting and about whatever can be done to animals because if we sympathize more with animals than with people hunters will no longer be allowed to shoot a moose or to go fishing and catch a good salmon.
